$comment: The element ontology is ORTHOGONAL to the style graph. Slots are universal; a style is a set of bindings and constraints on these slots. Georgian does not own a cornice — it specifies one. Adding a style must never require adding a slot; if it does, the ontology was incomplete, not the style exotic.

groups.name: Massing & Roof
groups.note: The skeleton. Inherits along a different axis than ornament — see massings/ catalog.

slots.name: Composition parti
slots.note: The whole-building compositional law: symmetry class, bay parity, where the centre is and whether there is one. Added in 0.2.0 — the Georgian exercise found that a style whose identity IS strict bilateral symmetry had nowhere to say so, and could not forbid a picturesque parti because no slot existed to forbid it in.

slots.name: Roof pitch
slots.note: One of the highest-signal, lowest-cost style tells. A 4:12 Georgian reads wrong at any level of trim quality.

slots.name: Eave condition
slots.note: Where the wall meets the sky. Boxed-and-returned, exposed rafter tail, closed soffit, flared, clipped — arguably the single most diagnostic detail in the whole kit.

slots.name: Chimney
slots.note: Position (central, gable-end, exterior-end, paired) is a plan-logic decision, not decoration. It is the fossil of the heating strategy.

slots.name: Storey proportion
slots.note: Ratio of ground-floor to upper-floor height; the graduation that makes a facade sit down rather than float.

slots.name: Construction type
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. The ontology recorded appearance and not construction, so nothing could state whether Flemish bond was physically possible or was half-bricks glued to a backup. Nearly every honest-material question resolves here.

slots.name: Wall thickness, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #12), the fourth and last of the same trade-conflation family as window_head, corner_treatment and window_surround (window_head_masonry/window_head_wood, corner_quoin/corner_board, window_surround_masonry/window_surround_wood, all split in 0.3.0) -- it had simply never been added as its own slot at all, under any name, before now. A solid-masonry or masonry-veneer wall's thickness is load-bearing geometry or a fixed veneer-plus-cavity-plus-backup buildup: 13-18 in for a two-wythe brick bearing wall, 18-30+ in for coursed stone, a veneer wall's own figure driven by code minimum cavity and backup rather than by any proportional module. Discriminate with construction_type.

slots.name: Wall thickness, frame
slots.note: Split in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #12), paired with wall_thickness_masonry. A framed wall's overall thickness is stud depth plus sheathing plus cladding plus interior finish -- typically 6-10 in for a 2x4 or 2x6 wall with modern insulation and siding -- and is a code and energy-code question, not a proportional one. The opposite assembly reaching a comparable overall dimension by a wholly different logic, the same relationship reveal_masonry/reveal_frame already models.

slots.name: Secondary cladding
slots.note: Material change is usually a storey-line or wing decision, never arbitrary.

slots.name: Material transition rule
slots.note: Where a material may change and what must occur at the joint. Prevents the 'brick blanket on the front only' pathology of production building.

slots.name: Corner quoin
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A quoin is an ORDER element governed by the masonry module. Applying its dimension to a framed corner is roughly 2x wrong, and did in fact produce a live bug in facade-classical.

slots.name: Corner board
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A corner board is TRIM, measured at 6-10 in on surviving frame work, and sized by the clapboard it terminates rather than by any module.

slots.name: Reveal, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. 4-8 in of reveal in a mass wall, with no architrave. The depth IS the expression, and it is what tells the eye the wall carries load.

slots.name: Reveal, frame
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. 3/4-2 in of reveal plus a 5-6 in architrave doing the work the depth cannot. The opposite assembly reaching the same effect.

slots.name: Main cornice
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). The entablature's own cornice component when a full classical apparatus is bound (`entablature` in Classical Apparatus) -- and it, `frieze`, `modillion_dentil`, `crown` and `chair_rail` are the same object at different scales, three of them literally the same run. This cross-reference is not a regrouping: every one of the six keeps its own id and every existing kit binding stays valid. Where no `entablature` is bound at all -- the common case, since most vernacular envelope-only Georgian work states cornice and frieze directly without a full engaged order -- `cornice` is the de facto standalone module source the other four should still agree with.

slots.name: Frieze
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). Sits directly below `cornice` in the same entablature run; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Rainwater strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Gutters and leaders ruin more traditional eaves than any other single element, and the eave slot is about the cornice.

slots.name: Colour strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Highly diagnostic, period-specific, and the cheapest thing on a house to get right or wrong.

slots.name: Window proportion
slots.note: Height:width of the sash opening. Governs whether a facade reads as vertical (traditional) or horizontal (modern default).

slots.name: Window head, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A gauged brick jack arch is the mason's: structural, cambered by roughly opening/96, four courses deep, laid up on a centre before the wall closes.

slots.name: Window head, wood
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. A moulded wood cap is the carpenter's: non-structural, nailed on after the wall is closed, and free to be any profile the plane can cut.

slots.name: Window surround, masonry
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type. In masonry Georgian the canonical value is NONE, and that is a design decision rather than an absence: the opening reads as a hole cut in a mass, and adding a surround destroys the reading.

slots.name: Window surround, wood
slots.note: Split in 0.3.0. The predecessor slot conflated two assemblies made by different trades, at different times, in different materials, with different failure modes. Discriminate with construction_type.

slots.name: Grouping & rhythm rule
slots.note: Singles, pairs, ribbons; bay spacing; alignment of upper to lower. The grammar of the facade.

slots.name: Shutter
slots.note: Must be sized to actually close over the opening, hung on real hardware. Half-width shutters are the most common single tell of a fake traditional facade.

slots.name: Door surround
slots.note: In most traditional styles the entry is the single most elaborated element. The surround is where the style declares itself.

slots.name: Garage strategy
slots.note: No historical precedent exists. Every traditional style needs an explicit, authored answer or the car eats the facade. This slot is where a modern kit-of-parts earns its keep.

slots.name: Glazing assembly
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Insulated glass changes muntin width, which changes the window, which is most styles' first tell. The trade-off needs somewhere to live.

groups.name: Classical Apparatus
groups.note: Only bound in styles within the classical stream. Vernacular and picturesque styles set these to 'forbidden' or leave open.

slots.name: Column / post
slots.note: Entasis, diminution, and plinth height are parametric and must scale with the order, not with the lumber yard.

slots.name: Entablature
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13): the root of a six-slot cross-reference family, not a regrouping. When bound, this IS the module source `cornice`, `frieze`, `modillion_dentil` (Envelope / Classical Apparatus), `crown` and `chair_rail` (Interior) should agree with -- see `cornice`'s note. This slot itself has no `derives_from_module`; it derives from the proportion pack's order, not from another slot.

slots.name: Modillion / dentil course
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). A coursework detail within the cornice band; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

groups.name: Porch & Threshold
groups.note: The mediating zone between public and private. In American residential architecture this is where the social contract of the street is written.

slots.name: Porch depth
slots.note: Depth decides what a porch IS, and different traditions want different answers. A Craftsman or Queen Anne porch below about 7 ft fails as an outdoor room; a Georgian entry portico is 5-6 ft and is a piece of the order rather than a room, and enlarging it to satisfy a Craftsman threshold makes it wrong. Bind the threshold in the style's kit, not here. (0.2.0: this note previously asserted the Craftsman figure as universal, which the Georgian authoring exercise caught.)

slots.name: Entry sequence
slots.note: Number of thresholds crossed from street to hall. Phenomenologically the most consequential decision in the whole kit and the one most often unmade.

slots.name: Trim profile family
slots.note: A single coherent profile family per style. Mixing families is the interior equivalent of mixing typefaces.

slots.name: Crown / cornice
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13). In high-style interior work this is the same run as the exterior cornice at a smaller scale, not an independently invented moulding; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

slots.name: Chair rail
slots.note: Added in 0.5.0 (docs/open-questions.md #13, the ruling's own named example). Its module should derive from the same run as the exterior cornice rather than being independently invented; see `cornice`'s note for how this cross-reference resolves when no `entablature` is bound.

groups.name: Plan Logic
groups.note: The deepest layer. Two houses can share every trim profile and still be different species if their plan logic differs.

slots.name: Room adjacency overrides
slots.note: Demoted in 0.4.0. The UNIVERSAL adjacency rules now live on the room records in rooms/, where they belong — they are properties of a dining room, not of Georgian. This slot holds only what a style ADDS or SUPPRESSES: Georgian permits chambers entered through one another, which the neutral rule forbids; the Creole cottage suppresses the corridor rule entirely. Same element-first-with-style-as-facet pattern as the fault corpus. A style that states a universal rule here is duplicating data that will drift.

slots.name: Storage strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Closets are a plan element and built-ins are joinery; they are not the same slot. Styles that predate the closet need an authored answer here.

slots.name: Mechanical & services strategy
slots.note: Added in 0.2.0. Chases, stacks, ducts, equipment. Where the plumbing stacks go decides whether a centre-passage plan survives contact with an MEP layout, and the ontology was silent on it.

groups.name: Site & Settlement
groups.note: A style is not only a building. Detached from its settlement pattern it becomes a costume.

slots.name: Grade relationship
slots.note: How the building meets the ground. Plinth, berm, cellar-exposure, terrace.
